newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia leader's Africa, Mideast "safari" slammed.
newsitem.headline: Colombia leader's Africa, Mideast "safari" slammed.

text.p: Colombia's President Ernesto Samper leaves for a 10-day official visit of Africa and the Middle East on Wednesday amid growing criticism that the trip is a waste of time and money.
Prominent political analysts have dubbed the tour of South Africa, Kenya, Israel, Palestine, Egypt, Morocco and Algeria as little more than an expensive "safari".
The opposition Conservative Party described the trip as an insult to millions of poor and unemployed Colombians.

But government officials defended the visit being carried out by Samper mainly in his capacity as head of the Non-Aligned Movement as an historic opportunity and the first by a Colombian president to the region.

"The president is once again going on a trip ... a safari to Africa. What a great way to demonstrate the government's desire to cut public spending! Are we maybe going to import more elephants or export monkeys," columnist Juan Lozano said in Colombia's leading El Tiempo newspaper on Monday. He quoted unnamed sources as saying Samper's party would include at least 90 people including Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia.
In January the government announced it would restrict foreign trips to rein in a fiscal deficit which was running at 4.1 percent of gross domestic product GDP last year.

Samper leaves Colombia on Wednesday and heads first to South Africa after a stop-over in Brazil. The official part of the tour concludes May 10 in Algeria but Samper will spend two days on a private visit to Madrid before returning to Bogota.

Political analyst Juan Tokatlian said Samper was using the 112-member Non-Aligned Movement as a vehicle to break Colombia's "international isolation" caused by the United States decision to blacklist the country for two consecutive years for its failure to crack down hard enough on drug trafficking.
